episodes.172881: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed in cyclonic northwest flow during the afternoon hours on Sunday (9/25).  The storms produced sub-severe wind gusts and hail across northeast Wisconsin.
episodes.173029: A weak cold front and strong upper level disturbance brought a line of strong to severe thunderstorms across southern WI for the late afternoon and early evening hours. Tree damage from straight-line winds was the most prevalent.
episodes.173089: With localized instability supporting their development, heavy showers formed over portions of Oahu and the Big Island.  The precipitation produced small stream and drainage ditch flooding, and ponding on roadways.  Some of the precipitation was heavy enough to cause flash flooding in leeward Big Island on the 25th. However, there were no reports of significant property damage or injuries.
episodes.173120: Residual moisture across southeast Utah fueled scattered thunderstorms across the region. Additionally, moderate instability led to some stronger thunderstorms; one of which produced a funnel cloud in Grand County.
episodes.173373: The combination of a potent shortwave aloft and a surface cold front provided a few rounds of showers and thunderstorms to the area on September 25th.  All of the storms remained sub-severe, save for one instance of large hail in Monongalia County.
episodes.173492: Strong to severe storms affected areas along and south of Highway 60 from the afternoon of the 23rd to the early morning of the 25th. The strongest storms developed during the afternoon of the 24th along Highway 60, and produced damaging wind gusts over 60 mph. Rainfall accumulations over two inches occurred over portions of south central Missouri from Mansfield to Winona.
episodes.173764: A shortwave moved from western Arkansas into the Mid-South and interacted with a moist and unstable airmass across the Delta region. Thunderstorms developed with several reports of damaging winds.

episodes.173854: Clusters of thunderstorms tracked east-southeast from Middle Tennessee and Kentucky during the afternoon hours of September 25. There were numerous reports of wind damage across the northern Cumberland Plateau and northeast Tennessee counties, mainly in the form of downed trees.
episodes.173934: A line of thunderstorms crossed the Mid-Susquehanna Valley during the early evening hours of September 25, 2022, as a cold front crossed the area. In spite of relatively modest instability, deep-layer shear was sufficient enough to produce isolated damaging winds within this line of storms.
episodes.174091: A warm front and trailing cold front swept across Central New York. One storm developed in the warm sector and dropped quarter sized hail in Broome County. This storm then weakened but became stronger again in Delaware County as it approached the warm front. The shear from the warm front was enough for a weak tornado to develop.
episodes.174092: A cold front associated with a low pressure system moved eastward into the Mid Atlantic region, and into the Virginia Piedmont. Southwesterly flow ahead of the front brought in additional warm, moist air into the region. Daytime heating increased atmospheric instability, with MLCAPEs reaching over 500 J/kg in some locations. Strong deep layer shear, around 50 knots, and decent mid-level moisture contributed to the development of scattered severe thunderstorms.
episodes.174093: A cold front associated with a low pressure system moved eastward into the Mid Atlantic and North Central North Carolina. Southwesterly flow ahead of the front brought in additional warm, moist air into the region, while daytime heating increased atmospheric instability, with MLCAPEs reaching over 500 J/kg in some locations. Strong deep layer shear, around 50 knots, and decent mid-level moisture contributed to the development of a few severe thunderstorms.
episodes.174124: A cold front moving southeast through middle Tennessee on September 25, 2022, helped to develop scattered showers and thunderstorms along it during the afternoon and evening hours. As the atmosphere destabilized, enough instability and wind shear was present to allow for a few strong thunderstorms, particularly along and east of the boundary. Across the Cumberland Plateau, a couple of sub-severe hail reports were received.
episodes.174173: An occluded surface low meandered in vicinity of Georgian Bay during the early afternoon of the 25th through early afternoon of the 26th. Multiple surface trough axes revolved around the low and moved generally southeastward through northern Ohio. These trough axes were accompanied by isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms, especially during the late morning through early evening of both the 25th and 26th, as the boundary layer destabilized via daytime heating. A couple of the thunderstorms produced hail up to penny-size. The ambient environment exhibited weak to moderate deep layer bulk shear and primarily weak MUCAPE.
episodes.174195: Northwesterly flow aloft aided in pushing a cold front southward into the region on the afternoon of September 25th. Despite only weak upper-level support, frontal forcing was sufficient to generate scattered convection along the frontal boundary during the afternoon. The atmosphere was relatively uncapped, and with afternoon temperatures climbing into the mid 90s, moderate surface-based instability developed. However, a lack of deep layer moisture appeared to be a limiting factor for any severe weather although classic inverted-V forecast soundings indicated the potential for isolated damaging wind gusts from thunderstorm downbursts in the afternoon. Moisture proved to be sufficient for storms to rapidly develop by mid to late afternoon, quickly accelerating southward and producing sporadic damaging wind gusts and large hail across parts of Southwest Arkansas.

The National Weather Service in Binghamton NY confirmed with a |storm survey, that a tornado moved through the Walton area on the |evening of September 25th between 6:38 PM to 6:41 PM. During the |survey, tornado damage was first noted along Walton Mountain Rd |where trees fell in a convergent pattern. Talking to several |residents, winds came from multiple directions, with lawn furniture|and part of a deck railing blown northwest while trees in |the back yard were blown down facing southwest. Sporadic tree |damage was followed down to route 10 to an autoshop with some |metal sheeting ripped off of the roof and thrown about a 100 |yards. From there the damage picked back up across the West Branch|of the Delaware River along S River Rd. Sporadic tree damage |continued along the south shore of the river to just south of S |river Rd with the worst tree damage occurring near the end of the |tornado's track. Up until this section, the damage from the |tornado was EF0. Many large trees were snapped or uprooted and |fell in a cross stitch pattern for a section of forest that was |about 300 yards long and 50 yards wide where the EF1 damage was |found.
